4. The facts giving rise to the impugned order of remand for retrial of the Suit can briefly be stated as follows:- One Khorshed Ahmed instituted the aforesaid title Suit in the first Court of Munsif', Kushtia for ejectment of his monthly tenant one Md. Zahed Ali and another Ukiluddin said to be a sub-tenant, from the suit premises alleging, inter alia, that the tenant was a defaulter created public nuisance in front of his residential house, sub-let the suit premises in contravention of the agreement of tenancy and that the landlord bonafide required the premises for his own use and occupation for making a drawing room. The tenant contested the suit denying all the material allegations in his written statement, The suit was decreed on contest with cost on 22.8.80 with the findings that :- (1) Notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served upon defendant No. 1 the tenant. (2) The tenant was a defaulter. (3) The plaintiff required the suit premises for his own use. (4) The barber shop in front of a residential house is a nuisance though not a public nuisance. (5) The plaintiff failed to prove sub-letting by-the tenant. 

 5. Against the decision of the Trial Court the tenant preferred Title Appeal No. 118 of 1980 before the learned District Judge, Kushtia who dismissed the appeal and affirmed the Judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 6. Thereupon the defendants filed provisional application before this Bench of the High Court Di- vision being Civil Revision Case No. 760 of 1981 against the said Judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court. The High Court Division vide Judgment and order dated 13.4.83 by Justice A.R. Chowdhury allowed the provisional application, set aside the Judgment and decree passed by Mr. M.A. Rahman, District Judge, Kushtia on 27.4.81 & 29.4.81 respectively and sent back the case on remand to that appellate court for rehearing in accordance with law in the light of evidence already on record and observation made therein. The Learned District Judge was further "directed to dispose of the appeal within 2 months of the date of receipt of the record from this Court". 

 7. The appeal thereafter was again heard by the District Judge who held :-(a) Defendant-appellant was not a defaulter having an un-adjusted amount of Tk. 6,800/- as security deposit with the landlord, (b) Running of a barber shop in the suit premises about 10/12 feet away from outside the main gate of the residential house, where there are other shops run by different tenants under him, was not a nuisance (c) Plaintiff landlord succeeded in proving the bonafide requirement for the suit premises for his use and occupation as a drawing room; (d) Regarding sub- letting or otherwise the lower appellate court in the absence of independent evidence, could not rely on the deposition of the tenant and defendant No.2 (alleged sub-tenant) to the effect' that the tenant runs the barber shop through his worker defendant No.2. However, two trade licenses appearing in the name of the tenant were produced before the learned District Judge to prove that it was not a case of sub- letting. The learned District Judge considered these documents "as very important" for the purpose of determining the question of sub-letting or otherwise and in that view of the matter, 'on 15.8.83 allowed the appeal, set aside the Judgment and decree of the trial Court and sent back the suit'; on remand for retrial after affording an opportunity to the defendant- appellants to prove into evidence the referred documents" for the purpose of deciding the point of sub- letting and also for deciding whether in the light of his observations and findings, the decree passed by the trial court was according to law. Further, considering that the suit was a long drawn one, the learned District Judge directed the trial court to dispose of it within one month of the receipt of the record. 

 11. Section 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure lays down that an appeal shall lie from the orders, enumerated therein and from no other orders "save as otherwise expressly provided in the body of this Code or any law for the time being in force." Order 43 of the Code which forms part of this section contains an enumeration of appealable orders and lays down in rule 1 that an appeal shall lie from the orders enumerated thereunder and clause (u) of that rule specifies in the list of appealable orders "an order under rule 23 of Order XLI remanding a case, where an appeal would lie from the decree of the Appellate Court." 

 12. So in order that an order of remand may be appealable two conditions need to be fulfilled:- (i) that the order of remand has been passed under Order 41, rule 23 i.e. when the lower court has disposed of the suit on a preliminary point and the appellate Court finds that the decision of that Court is wrong, and (ii) where the decree of the appellate Court is appealable. 

 13. In the instant case it is obvious that the order of remand was not passed by the learned District Judge under Order 41, rule 23 as the trial Court did not dispose of the suit on a preliminary point but decreed the suit on clear findings on all the issues raised therein. 

 14. Regarding the fulfillment of the second condition i.e. "where an appeal would lie from the decree of appellate Court", it cannot be said now after the omission of section 100 of the Code since 1.6.79 by the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978 (Ordinance XLIX of 1978), that this condition can ever be fulfilled as an appeal does not lie now from the decree of the appellate Court. So, even if an order of remand is passed now under Order 41, rule 23, appeal will not lie against such an order of remand under section 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Order 43 as the second condition referred to above would not be fulfilled.
